A1:
Exam weight: 4 recalled questions (2 of 5 sessions) — Brief. Asked as statement sets on characteristics, advantages and channels.

1. Key idea

Retail banking means banking services for individuals and small businesses — deposits, loans, cards, payments and investment products — delivered in large volumes of small-value transactions through many channels (branches, ATMs, internet, mobile, agents).

2. Characteristics, advantages, constraints

CharacteristicsAdvantages to the bankConstraints / challenges
• Mass market — very large customer base
• High volume, low value per transaction
• Wide range of both liability and asset products, plus service products
• Multiple delivery channels (physical + electronic)
• Standardised products, often scored/automated decisions		 • Stable, low-cost deposits (CASA)
• Credit risk well diversified — many small loans
• Better spreads — customers are too fragmented to bargain
• Mass marketing and cross-selling are easier with a large base
• Fee income from cards, payments, third-party products		 • High cost of servicing many small accounts
• Heavy technology investment and cyber-security risk
• Intense competition (banks, NBFCs, fintechs)
• Customers switch easily — low loyalty
• Appraisal and recovery of many small loans is laborious
• Manpower and skill gaps; regulatory compliance (KYC, conduct)
Traps seen: "Retail banking offers a limited range of liability products" (wrong — wide range of both, May 25-Q1) · "Retail banking primarily serves medium-sized businesses, not individuals" (wrong) · "Customers frequently switch banks" is listed as an advantage (it is a constraint, May 25-Q2).

3. Evolution and future

  • Before 1990s PSBs focused on deposits and priority/corporate lending; retail loans were small.
  • Retail banking gained momentum after 1991 liberalisation — entry of new private and foreign banks, technology (core banking, ATMs, cards) and rising middle-class incomes. The IIBF book traces the retail push to the entry of foreign banks (PYQ Jun 24-Q5 answer: Citibank for the first credit card).
  • Benefits of digital banking (Jun 24-Q6 — answer "all"): 24×7 availability, instant transactions, financial inclusion of the unbanked, lower cost for banks.
  • Prerequisites for success: technology-enabled multi-channel delivery, CRM and customer data, product innovation, efficient credit appraisal and recovery, cost control, trained staff.
  • Future: digital-first and mobile banking, AI-based personalisation, open banking/account aggregators, fintech partnerships, neo-banks.

4. Not yet asked — know briefly

Constraints list (above) · prerequisites for success · future of retail banking. Expect a "Which is NOT a constraint / prerequisite" question.

2. Profit vs profitability

  • Profit is an absolute amount = total revenue − total expenses.
  • Profitability is relative — return earned on the resources/investment used (e.g., ROA, ROE). A bank can have high profit but low profitability.
LevelFormula
Gross profitSales − Cost of goods sold
Operating profitGross profit − Operating expenses (selling, general & admin)
Net profitOperating profit − Interest − Taxes
For a bank: Net Interest Income (NII) = Interest earned − Interest expended · Operating profit = NII + Other (non-interest) income − Operating expenses · Net profit = Operating profit − Provisions & contingencies − Tax

3. Ratios (formula bank)

RatioFormulaReading
ROANet profit ÷ Average total assetsHigher = better use of assets
ROENet profit ÷ Average shareholders' equityROE = ROA × (Assets ÷ Equity) — leverage raises ROE
NIMNII ÷ Average earning assetsCore lending margin
Cost-to-income (efficiency) ratioOperating expenses ÷ (NII + Other income)Lower = more efficient
Margin (GP / OP / NP)Respective profit ÷ Sales × 100
SpreadYield on advances − Cost of deposits
Worked: Assets ₹45 lakh at start, ₹55 lakh at end, net income ₹75,000 → average assets = (45 + 55) ÷ 2 = ₹50 lakh → ROA = 0.75 ÷ 50 = 1.5% (May 26-Q2). Trap options use opening (1.67%) or closing (1.36%) assets.
Worked: Fees revenue ₹8,00,000; direct cost ₹3,50,000; SG&A ₹1,50,000; interest ₹50,000; tax ₹60,000 → GP 4,50,000 → OP 3,00,000 → NP 1,90,000 → NP margin = 23.75% (Nov 25-Q6).

4. Non-interest (fee) income

Commission and fees: custodial fees, underwriting commissions, insurance and MF distribution commissions (cross-selling), locker rent, processing fees, remittance and card fees, forex income. Interest on a cash credit is interest income, not fee income (Nov 25-Q9).

CRR balances with RBI earn no interest — a drag on profitability (May 26-Q6). SLR investments do earn interest.

5. Improving branch profitability

  • Relentless focus on NPA reduction and recovery; raise CASA share (cheaper funds).
  • Grow fee income and cross-selling; deepen customer relationships.
  • Control operating costs without hurting customer service; use technology and alternate channels; improve staff productivity.
  • The best approach balances operating efficiency with capability upgrades — cost-cutting alone is not sustainable (May 25-Q8).

Factors affecting profitability of Indian banks: NPAs and provisions, cost of deposits, interest-rate movements, competition, operating costs and staff expenses, regulatory pre-emptions (CRR/SLR, priority sector), technology.

Traps seen: "Cost cutting at the expense of customer satisfaction" improves profitability (it does not, Jun 24-Q3) · "Profitability is an absolute term" (Oct 24-Q1) · Gross profit = Sales − operating expenses (wrong, Oct 24-Q5) · "Commercial banks get 3% on CRR" (wrong, May 26-Q6) · higher efficiency ratio taken as better (wrong, Nov 25-Q4).

1. Credit score basics

  • A credit score is a 3-digit statistical summary of a person's past credit behaviour — their credit discipline.
  • Range: 300 to 900. Higher is better; above about 750 is considered good. The IIBF content quoted in Nov 25-Q30: CIBIL above 700 → about 90% approval chance.
  • Banks use the Credit Information Report (CIR) when processing retail loans (May 26-Q12).
  • Score drivers: repayment history · credit utilisation · length of credit history · credit mix · number of recent enquiries.
  • Hurts the score: missed EMIs, paying only the minimum due on cards, high utilisation, many enquiries, "settled" accounts, default as a guarantor.
  • Evolution: statistical scoring began in the USA (FICO); CIBIL (India's first CIC) was set up in 2000.
  • Scoring models use the borrower's character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions (5 Cs).

1. Key idea

Deposits are the bank's liabilities — money the bank owes to customers. They come in two kinds: demand deposits (withdraw any time) and time deposits (withdraw after a fixed period). The bank is the debtor and the depositor is the creditor.

PointDemand depositsTime (term) deposits
AccountsCurrent account (CA), Savings account (SB)Fixed deposit (FD), Recurring deposit (RD)
WithdrawalAny time, on demandAfter a fixed term (premature allowed with penalty, as per bank policy)

Traps seen: "RD is a demand deposit" (wrong, Jun 24-Q18) · "Home loan is a liability product" (wrong — it is an asset product, Oct 24-Q16) · "Credit card is a liability product" (wrong, Nov 25-Q25) · Banker–depositor relation is debtor–creditor, not agent–principal or trustee–beneficiary (Jun 24-Q23).

2. Current account

  • Meant for businesses and frequent transactors. No interest is paid.
  • No restriction on the number or amount of deposits/withdrawals.
  • Does not promote the saving habit.
  • Credit exposure rule (RBI): a borrower whose total exposure across the banking system is below ₹5 crore may open current accounts freely, but must inform the bank(s) once exposure reaches ₹5 crore or more (May 25-Q20).
  • Closure: on the customer's written request (unused cheque leaves returned). A bank may close an unsatisfactorily conducted account after giving notice.
Trap seen (Oct 24-Q33): all three features were written as their opposites — "interest-bearing", "restriction on deposits", "promotes saving". Answer: None of the above.

3. Savings bank account

  • Who can open: individuals (single/joint), minors (see section 5), and non-profit bodies such as associations, clubs, trusts and societies. Not meant for trading/business entities.
  • Interest deregulated on 25 October 2011 — banks set their own SB rate, under a Board-approved policy.
  • Up to ₹1 lakh: one uniform rate. Above ₹1 lakh: banks may pay differential rates.
  • Interest is calculated on the daily product (end-of-day balance) and credited at quarterly or shorter intervals.
  • Services: debit card, internet/mobile banking, standing instructions, sweep facility, nomination.
Traps seen: "Uniform rate till ₹50,000" (wrong figure, Jun 24-Q15) · "Rate policy approved by branch managers" (wrong — Board, Nov 25-Q8) · "Uniform rate on the entire balance" (wrong — differential allowed above ₹1 lakh).

6. Basic Savings Bank Deposit Account (BSBDA) NEW from 1 April 2026

  • Replaced the old "no-frills" account (RBI, August 2012). It is a normal banking service available to all, subject to KYC.
  • No minimum balance and no initial deposit.
  • Free ATM-cum-debit card (no issue or renewal charge).
  • At least 4 free withdrawals per month, including ATM withdrawals.
  • NEW Digital transactions — UPI, NEFT, IMPS, RTGS, PoS payments — are not counted in the 4 withdrawals.
  • No limit on deposits. Reactivating an inoperative BSBDA is free.
  • A BSBDA holder cannot have any other savings account in the same bank.

Source of the 2026 changes: RBI BSBDA Amendment Directions, 4 December 2025, effective 1 April 2026 (within the 30 June 2026 cut-off). Older questions (e.g. May 25-Q10 "maximum four withdrawals including ATM") were set before this change — read the question carefully for whether it is testing the old or new framing.

8. KYC

  • Legal basis: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and the PML Rules, 2005; RBI KYC Master Direction.
  • KYC policy approved by the Board of Directors (trap: "Head of Retail Banking", Nov 25-Q19).
  • Four elements: Customer Acceptance Policy · Risk Management · Customer Identification Procedure · Monitoring of Transactions.
  • If Customer Due Diligence (CDD) is not possible because the customer will not cooperate → do not open the account. No fictitious/benami names.
  • Periodic KYC update: high risk every 2 years · medium risk every 8 years · low risk every 10 years (Nov 25-Q22 case).
  • Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR): functions performed by CERSAI (asked Oct 24-Q15 and May 25-Q17).
  • V-CIP (video KYC): live video, geo-tagging/GPS stamp, and an audit trail is mandatory (trap Jun 24-Q16).
  • Documents for an SB account: proof of identity (OVD), proof of address if different, photograph, PAN or Form 60.
  • Transfer of account to another branch of the same bank: KYC already done is valid; a fresh full KYC is not needed (self-declaration if address changed).

9. Inoperative accounts and unclaimed deposits

  • Inoperative: no customer-induced transaction for 2 years. Bank-credited interest or charges do not count. Activation is free.
  • Unclaimed for 10 years or more: amount is transferred to RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness (DEA) Fund; the customer can still claim it from the bank later.
Trap seen (Nov 25-Q18): "nil balance for 6 months" or "KYC not updated" — neither makes an account inoperative. Only 2 years without customer transactions.

SB interest on daily product. Balance ₹40,000 for 20 days, then ₹80,000 for 10 days, rate 3% p.a.
Daily product = 40,000 × 20 + 80,000 × 10 = 8,00,000 + 8,00,000 = 16,00,000

Premature withdrawal. FD ₹2,00,000 booked for 3 years at 7%. Closed after 1 year. Card rate for 1 year when booked = 6.5%; penalty = 1%.
Rate paid = rate for the period actually run − penalty = 6.5% − 1% = 5.5% (not 7% − 1%). Simple interest for 1 year = ₹11,000.

Overdue deposit. FD ₹1,00,000 at 6.5% matured and stayed unpaid for 6 months; SB rate 3%.

TDS. Mr. Arun (45, PAN given) earns ₹60,000 FD interest in a year from one bank. It exceeds ₹50,000, so TDS applies on the whole ₹60,000: 10% = ₹6,000 (not 10% of the ₹10,000 excess). Without PAN: 20% = ₹12,000.

2. Mortgage — types and registration

Equitable mortgage (mortgage by deposit of title deeds)Registered (simple / English) mortgage
Created by depositing title deeds with intent to create security — Sec 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 · only in notified towns · no mortgage deed needed, so no registration of a deed (some States require a memorandum to be registered or stamped) · cheaper and quicker · the most common form for home loansCreated by a mortgage deed signed by the mortgagor and attested by two witnesses · must be registered with the Sub-Registrar under the Registration Act, 1908 · stamp duty payable · used where the property is outside a notified town or the bank's policy demands it
  • A document must be presented for registration within 4 months of execution (Registration Act, Sec 23).
  • Priority: mortgages rank in order of date of creation; a later registered or notified charge cannot override an earlier one, so the bank checks encumbrances before disbursement.
  • CERSAI (Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India): every equitable mortgage and other security interest must be registered on CERSAI within 30 days of its creation. A CERSAI search before sanction reveals existing charges — the key defence against multiple financing on the same property. Registration gives the bank priority over later unregistered claims and is needed for SARFAESI enforcement.
  • Director's personal property mortgaged for a company loan: the mortgage by the director is personal, so it is registered with the Sub-Registrar/CERSAI — a charge filing with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) applies only to the company's own assets.

3. Frauds and how to detect forged deeds

  • Common home-loan frauds: forged or fake title deeds; the same property mortgaged to several banks; inflated valuations; fake salary slips/ITRs; impersonation of the owner; builder–borrower collusion with diversion of funds; disbursement for non-existent projects.
  • Detecting a forged deed: verify the original with the Sub-Registrar's records (certified copy), take a fresh encumbrance certificate, search CERSAI, check stamp-paper serial numbers and vendor, compare signatures and photographs, check that the chain of title is unbroken, conduct a site visit and talk to neighbours/society, insist on originals (not photocopies).

4. Monitoring and closure

  • Post-disbursement: end-use check, stage-wise site inspections, property insured against fire and natural calamities with the bank's interest noted, periodic review of the account (SMA tracking).
  • Interest-rate reset (RBI, 2023): at the time of reset the borrower must be given the option to switch to a fixed rate, enhance EMI, extend tenor or prepay; the bank cannot extend tenor beyond the borrower's capacity without consent.
  • Prepayment: no foreclosure or prepayment charges on floating-rate loans to individuals (non-business).
  • Release of documents on closure (RBI, effective 1 December 2023): original property documents must be released, and any charge registered with CERSAI removed, within 30 days of full repayment. For delay attributable to the bank, compensation is ₹5,000 per day of delay. If documents are lost or damaged, the bank must help obtain duplicate/certified copies and bear the costs, and gets an extra 30 days (60 days in total) to do so. The borrower may collect documents from the branch where the loan was serviced or any other office having them.

2. Time value of money

ConceptFormula
Future valueFV = PV × (1 + r)n

Worked example: ₹10 lakh at 9% for 10 years → r = 0.0075, n = 120 → EMI ≈ ₹12,668. Total paid ≈ ₹15.2 lakh, so total interest ≈ ₹5.2 lakh. First month's interest = 10,00,000 × 0.0075 = ₹7,500; principal = 12,668 − 7,500 = ₹5,168.

Amortisation: each EMI = interest on the outstanding balance + principal. Early EMIs are mostly interest; later EMIs are mostly principal. When rates rise, banks usually extend the tenor rather than raise the EMI, which can sharply increase total interest. Flat rate (interest on the original principal throughout) costs much more than the same reducing-balance rate.

1. Who values and how

  • Valuation is done by the bank's empanelled valuers (registered valuers — e.g., registered with IBBI under Sec 247 of the Companies Act, or under the Wealth-tax/Income-tax rules), independent of the sales and sanctioning staff. Banks set rotation and second-valuation rules in their Board-approved policy.

2. Land, buildings, depreciation

  • Belting method for large plots: land near the road (front belt) is worth more; the plot is divided into belts by depth, the front belt valued at the full rate and the rear belts at lower rates (for example two-thirds and one-half).
  • Life of structures: RCC framed structures last longest (about 60–75 years), load-bearing structures less, temporary/semi-permanent structures much less; the remaining life drives the depreciation.
  • Straight-line depreciation (SLM): annual depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life. Depreciated value = cost − annual depreciation × age.
  • Sinking fund: the amount set aside every year, earning interest, to replace the building at the end of its life. Annual instalment = replacement cost × i ÷ [(1 + i)n − 1].

PaymentsBank pays the borrower — monthly, quarterly, annually or lump sum; loan amount based on property value, age and interest rate
Maximum period20 years
RevaluationProperty revalued at least once every 5 years; payments may be revised
RepaymentNo repayment during the borrower's (and spouse's) lifetime; they can live in the house till death. Loan settled by sale of the property or by heirs repaying with interest; any surplus goes to the heirs
TaxAmounts received are a loan, not income — exempt (Sec 10(43)); mortgaging is not a "transfer" for capital gains (Sec 47(xvi))
